t: Nobody called us crazy the second time.

In 2021 — as the Covid-19 vaccines were just rolling out, but RJ and I weren’t yet comfortable with flying — we drove 26 hours over three days, back home to the east coast, to meet our niece for the first time before her first birthday. Everyone thought we'd lost our minds. “You drove 26 hours from Denver? You guys are crazy.” (Then those same people complained about us not staying for long enough, despite us being around for eight weeks.)
Crazy. Sure. We wore it like a badge of honor, like we were the kind of people who take the long way on purpose because it’s a way to get it done, and doing it together is an adventure.

In 2023, we made the same drive. Same 26 hours, give or take. Two days. Arguably crazier than the first time. This time, when we mentioned it to people, they just nodded. “Of course you did. What else would you do?”
Crazy, it turns out, is a word for choices. This one didn't feel like a choice at all.

My mother-in-law died on Christmas Eve, 2022. My father-in-law died six months and two weeks later, in July 2023. I am sure of this fact because Mom often huffed, “You couldn’t last six months without me.” Dad proved her wrong, if only by a few weeks.

Neither RJ nor I remember actually deciding to pack up the car for a trip with no definite end date. We just mobilized. The actions arrived swiftly, without much discussion. We are both eldest children who shoulder the burden of responsibility. We just suck it up and get things done.
I've thought about that a lot since: how the biggest decision of that year actually wasn't a decision. It was a given. It was a responsibility. One we could have shirked, but we really couldn’t have.

Responsibility mode is a place I go alone, even with someone sitting right next to me. It hands me a task list to fulfill instead of a feeling to sit with. RJ was there, driving the other half of the shift, but the list was mine — mine to build, mine to hide inside. We had a plan, and I executed it like a job I'd been hired for. We didn't fight in the car, even though we would have been justified — we were tired and sitting side by side every waking hour of the day, driving on the same boring interstate for hours on end.
Looking back, I don't think competence is the same as being ok. I think I mistook one for the other for four months. Grief hadn't found the door yet. I made myself too busy to answer it anyway.

After Dad’s funeral in July, we flew home to Denver and immediately packed to leave again. We were in shraddha — the period after a death when the family observes certain traditions to protect and support the spirits of the deceased as they transition to higher realms. The idea, as I understood it, is that the person isn’t gone yet. They’re in transit. You mourn, yes, but you also sacrifice to ensure they make it to the afterlife. The way I’ve explained this period is comparing it to sitting shiva.

Apparently the traditions vary from Indian state to state, maybe town to town. For us, it lasted 13 days. You don't eat meat. You don’t cut your hair or nails. You don't celebrate. You wait, while somewhere unseen, a longer trip than yours is underway. And on the 13th day, you celebrate life.

While playing my role of passenger princess, I opened my map apps and started optimizing. Figuring out the best route (yep, it was still I-70), gas stops, places to eat — and it had to be vegetarian — before we both got too hangry to be reasonable. It felt productive. It felt like the responsible thing, the eldest-child thing, to handle the logistics, to keep the trip running smoothly.

It was also the only way I knew how to not talk about what we were driving toward. Not the house. Not what "a few months" of estate work might actually mean. Not what four months of that, stacked on top of our actual jobs, might do to us. I solved a logistics problem instead of an actual one, over and over, because a logistics problem has an answer. The other kind doesn't really.
The car smelled like greasy fast food, two greasy people, and one probably greasy dog — the perfume of a family living inside an Audi A5 Sportback instead of a house.

I’ve never had to think about vegetarian fast food options, so eating was an interesting part of the journey. It’s funny that McDonald's, Burger King, and Arby’s were considered interesting. Egg McMuffins are a solid breakfast choice; I learned that I might like them more without a sausage patty. The Impossible Whopper was a pleasant surprise (though very salty, as could be expected from fast food). There wasn’t much to choose from at Arby’s, so it was more like a meal made up of all sides — but the sides were delicious. Their mozz sticks and curly fries may be the best things on the menu. What a depressing way to learn how good the mozz sticks and curly fries are.

Kona got some of everything. She always does on road trips. She’s a great traveler and is always rewarded for it, usually with fries disappearing to the back seat. There's a version of those two days where I remember mostly anxious anticipation and exhaustion. There's another version, just as true, where I remember a dog’s chin on the center console, waiting, while RJ drove and I fed her fries one at a time like it was a fun vacation road trip. Except it wasn’t.

Indiana is always the worst part of any drive east. I couldn't tell you what it is about that state's asphalt specifically, but you feel every mile of it in your teeth. You know things are bad when you find yourself genuinely excited to cross into Ohio (oh, smooth roads! How we’ve missed thee!) which tells you everything about how low the bar had gotten. It is possible to be grieving and also delighted by pavement. Both were true. I don't think that's a contradiction. I think that's just what the umpteenth hour of a trip like this actually feels like.
We pulled into the driveway in the early evening of the second day. I don’t remember how I felt when we arrived, other than relieved we were no longer in the car.
The house was exactly as it had been left — mail still on the counter, nothing staged. The stillness of a place that still expected its people to come back to it.

The neighborhood was a 55+ community: cookie-cutter houses, manicured cul-de-sacs, a clubhouse with a fountain. We were in our suburban nightmare. Somewhere down the block, sprinklers ran on a timer for a lawn nobody was outside to enjoy. We parked the Audi — dog hair, fast-food bags, and all — in a driveway built for people who'd already finished the hard part of their lives.
We were about to start the hardest part of ours.
I had two full-time jobs that summer, and only one of them paid me.

RJ had bought a rinky-dink standing desk for his parents' house, for when he was working there while taking care of his mom in her final months. It wasn't fancy by any means, but it was tall enough to stand at and it was adjustable. It fit the most basic description of a standing desk.

I commandeered it and moved it into my father-in-law's office. I can't remember why. Maybe it was too hot upstairs in the summer. Maybe it was to be closer to the kitchen. But there was a reason, and it did strike me as odd that I set up my own cheap plastic desk next to my father-in-law's large wooden one.
And every day, I said good morning to coworkers in California who had no idea I was 1,800 miles from my own desk, or why, or what was a few feet behind my left shoulder.

I had just started a new job, so I immersed myself in work. Not only because I had to have a strong first 30-60-90 days, but also because I needed a distraction from the life I found myself in. I got good at The Voice: the bright, capable, mildly caffeinated voice that says "happy to jump on a call" and sounds like it means it. And as soon as a meeting ended, I was able to exhale. We all do a version of corporate theater, but this particular act was hiding a lot under the surface. I was not happy to jump on a call. I was not happy at all.

Because I had colleagues in California, I didn't close my work laptop until around 8pm. I’d take a quick break to run out to the kitchen at 5:30 and throw something together, eat it, and go back to work.
Then the other job started.

There was no boundary between them. Just a laptop closing and reopening — project launch plans swapped for spreadsheets of accounts to close, a coworker's Slack message for a banker’s email. Evenings were for the estate, and so were most weekends.

At some point I made a kanban board on the office wall, next to the desks. Post-its and three columns: To Do, In Progress, Done. I am a project manager. It's what I know how to do with a problem, and I didn't have another idea.
The columns didn't behave the way columns are supposed to. Stickies went into To Do and stayed there. In Progress got crowded. Done stayed thin for a long time.

We had tasks, but didn't really have a system. We picked whichever corner was closest to whatever we noticed that day, and we worked outward from there until we had just enough left in us to watch something stupid on TV and go to bed. Then it was morning, and coworkers wanted to know if I was happy to jump on a call. I was still not happy to jump on a call.

I stopped being able to tell you what day it was without checking. Tuesday and Saturday felt like different versions of the same day. I wore the same clothes, from the one suitcase of clothes I packed. I lost the part of a week that tells you when to rest, and didn't notice it was gone until much later.

We divided the work without ever discussing it. There were things I couldn't do, because they required deciding what something was worth, and I did not have that in me. So I took the boring ones. I did the admin. I did the grunt work of discarding expired pantry ingredients. I organized papers and notebooks and electronics chargers. I sorted things into piles and moved the piles into the state I thought of as “ready for a decision”.
RJ made the calls on what stayed and what went. I built the piles he had to stand in front of.

We lived in that house together and often missed each other in it. Not on purpose — there just weren’t many moments built for two people to be in the same room without a task attached to it. I'd hear him on a call through the wall, and he'd hear me. We'd pass in the kitchen reaching for the same leftovers, ask each other how it was going as if we were coworkers who liked each other just fine. We each had our list of things to get through during the day. Practicality took over most days.

I deciphered Dad's password notebook. He'd written all of them down by hand, and most of them didn't make any sense to me — English letters spelling words I didn't know. I asked RJ if any of it made sense, and he laughed. The passwords were in Odia, the language of Odisha, where his parents were from. The password to Macy's included the Odia word for shopping. TripAdvisor’s included the word for travel. On and on like that, a whole life's worth of logins in a language I don't speak, in a notebook I could read and not understand.
So that's how I spent my evenings. Deactivating accounts one at a time, while learning Odia words I cannot recall today.

I called his travel agent to cancel his upcoming trip to India. She was kind about it, said she was sorry for our loss, and then explained what she'd need to process the refund. I had to send her a copy of the death certificate. There is something strange about producing a document to prove you aren't running a scam with your father-in-law's death.

And there was the safe. The giant, hulking safe. We never got it open. The safe combo was not written anywhere in the password book; I tried every string of numbers I could see there. We could only try a certain number of combinations before it locked us out for the day. I didn't — still don’t — know how many digits are in the combination, so I was guessing at a number of unknown length a few tries at a time, every day, for a while, until I stopped.

My body kept its own tally, as it does. My feet ached by 3pm most days, and I couldn't tell you if that was from standing at that desk or from months of just generally bracing. Grief and overwork produce a remarkably similar physical signature, it turns out. I couldn't always locate, in my own body, which one I was actually feeling. Both, probably.

There were a few nights we just… didn't. Closed the laptop, didn't open anything else, sat there. It felt like relief and it felt like guilt, in roughly equal amounts, which meant it wasn't really either one. Or both, probably.
Four months. I took maybe a single day off in that timeframe.

The neighbors watched us throughout all of this. They were nosy and bored and, to their credit, just trying to be friendly. And there was no hiding from them: we were outside constantly, because Kona needed walking regardless of what kind of day either of us was having. So three times a day we'd loop the neighborhood — Turret Drive, Diamond Spring Drive, Constitution Drive, all the drives — with our dog who was just happy to be with us. Inevitably, we'd run into a neighbor who'd either 1) ask how cleaning out the house was going or 2) tell the same story about one of my in-laws.

One of them always wanted to talk about Kona, because RJ's first shiba, Misa, had lived in that house with his parents for the last few years of her life. So this neighbor knew exactly what a shiba was, and had known one on that street before. She'd say something about Misa, and I'd say something about Kona, and I suppose that was a conversation I was more willing to have than one about my late in-laws.

We were, by far, the youngest people living on that street. I understood, eventually, that we were the most interesting thing that had happened in that neighborhood in a while. I didn't love being someone's daytime television. But I couldn't really blame them, either. If I lived in that 55+ community, I probably would have watched us too.

I ask myself now how I did it — two jobs, no boundary between grief and inbox, four months with no exit date. The honest answer is I don't remember deciding to keep going. I just kept opening the laptop, whichever one. Some hours I couldn't have told you if I was working or grieving, or performing whichever version of myself could do either one without sitting down.

I used to think of myself as someone who was good under pressure. That summer I learned pressure doesn't test you so much as it erases whatever parts of you it doesn't currently need. What was left standing wasn't calm. It was just the part of me that still knew how to open a laptop and do whatever it was I needed to do.
We packed our standing desk in our moving pod. We packed the safe, too, still locked.
I don't remember what happened to Dad's desk.
We found three pizza cutters.

Mom had bought a new one every time she couldn't find the old one, and she never once found the old one, because there were so many kitchen tools spread across so many drawers. It was just easier to buy a new one. The old one was two drawers over the whole time. The second old one was too, I think.
Nobody in that house was hiding anything. They just kept adding.
I think about those pizza cutters more often than I'd like to admit. A whole life accumulates like that — not by decision, but by not-finding. Or not remembering what you had in the first place.

Eight spatulas. Seven wooden spoons. Six ladles. (And a partridge in a pear tree.) We had to decide what to do with all of it. Not only the kitchen utensils, but all of it. All 2,300 square feet of it.
… including the attic above the garage.

Vintage Corelle. Serving sets for the few times a year they had people over. Sterno burners for the same. Unopened gift sets — the ones you get and don't need or like and can't throw away, so you say thank you and store them in the attic for the next time you need a quick generic gift for someone. Wrapping paper for all occasions. Bins of clothing. Christmas decorations I had never seen. I don't know if they forgot about them or just stopped getting them down. More kitchen utensils, as though the drawers downstairs had overflowed and we'd found the runoff.
The kitchen drawers had recipes in them too, in Mom's handwriting.
One was for pani puri, on a single pink Post-it. 4 cups maida. 1 cup suji. Make the dough, roll it out, fry it.
That's the whole recipe written down — just the puris, and nothing about the filling or the pani. The rest, I assume, lived in her hands.
I've never tried making them.
My in-laws called me Ma: a term of endearment for a daughter.

Mom and I talked about cooking, and gardening, and we watched the Game Show Network together. She loved Family Feud. We'd fold laundry and heckle the contestants, and laugh at Steve Harvey laughing at the contestants too.
She often made chicken curry and aloo gobi (potatoes and cauliflower) when we visited, because she knew they were my favorites. They were not RJ's favorites at all.
RJ and I didn't learn until after she was gone that she didn't like potatoes. She made them anyway, for years.

There were hundreds of saris. I don't know the real number, and I lost count every time I tried. Silk, cotton, chiffon, polyester? Everyday ones, fancy ones, wedding ones. Some on hangers in the guest room closet. Most folded in stacks, in bags, in boxes, in the attic, tucked inside other bags, in a way that things belonging to a woman who kept everything are kept.

I took over the upstairs loft with them. The sofa, the chair, and the coffee table were all covered in piles of saris. There were large Rubbermaid containers packed full of saris too. I left one small corner of the couch empty so I could sit somewhere while sifting through them.
I sorted them by type, at first. Casual over here, fancy over there, silk in one pile, sheer in another. It was a good system.
I found an old suitcase in the attic, very old-timey looking. I think it was red and leather (or fake leather?). Thick handles. No wheels. I wondered what was in it.
More saris.
There was no theme to the saris in that suitcase. I think the theme was they just needed somewhere to go.

I kept finding more throughout the house, and at some point, the system just stopped being a system. Casual and fancy fell into each other. The silk pile grew a sheer layer. I couldn't tell you how I managed to sort through them, but I can tell you the loft looked like a sari shop after a sale.
We gave each auntie one of Mom's saris. That was RJ's decision.

Most of them asked for "this sari she wore at so-and-so's wedding," accompanied by a photo of the two of them at said wedding. Then I'd go upstairs and dig through the piles for a pattern in a photo, holding a phone up next to the fabric like I was matching paint swatches at a hardware store.
What was left was mine to decide. It was the first thing in that house that was.
My rule was: would I wear this? Not "did she love it?" Not "what is this worth?" Would I, Amanda, actually put this on? I make it a point to wear a sari to every Indian wedding we attend.
Every other question in that house was about something that had already happened.

RJ would come up to the loft every so often to see if there was anything he could do to help. The only help I accepted was asking him questions. "Should I keep this one?" or, "This one is really pretty. Do you know what she wore it to?"
Sometimes he knew. The ones he recognized were ones he'd just seen, going through old photos of her.

I kept most of the silk ones. Those were the ones I would actually wear. I loved the smooth, cool feel of the silk, as well as the colors and patterns. Many of them were Odia-style ikat saris — somehow they seemed to be the most "her".
The rest of them went to RJ’s sister. It worked out well, since she didn’t like wearing the silk saris anyway.
I found a stack of letters in Dad's office. Handwritten, from friends in India, going back decades. Mostly to Dad, I think. Some in Odia, some in English. Of course I read the ones in English.
Some were from people I know. Aunties and uncles I've sat across from at weddings, people I love, writing to a version of my father-in-law who was decades younger than any version I ever met.
In one of them, an uncle told Dad how much he loved meeting Mom.
I sat down on the floor of Dad's office and read every letter I actually could. I didn't sort them. I didn't build a pile. I didn't move anything into "ready for a decision." I kept all of them.
I did not have a breakdown.

I keep waiting, in this retelling, to arrive at the part where I fell apart. There wasn't one. I was in survival mode, which is not a feeling, it's an operating system. You don't cry in survival mode — or if you do, it's a blip, and you brush yourself off and carry on. The closest thing to a feeling is… numb.
When I did cry, it wasn't about them.

It was that I was tired, and overwhelmed, and sick of living in a house that wasn't mine, surrounded by things that weren't mine, eating at a table that wasn't mine. RJ and I said it to each other out loud more than once — how much we missed our own space, our own stuff. That was the thing big enough to cry about. Which was strange, since the only reason we were there at all was that two people had died.
I don't think I had room to cry about the second thing yet.
This September, more than three years later, we went to RJ's cousin's wedding in Jersey. I packed two of Mom's saris to wear: a fuchsia one for the ceremony, and a peacock blue one for the reception.
I can drape a sari myself (YouTube is my favorite school), but it takes me, I don't know, 40 minutes with many do-overs. An auntie can do it in ten minutes.

Before every one of these events, Mom would be the one who dressed me in a sari someone had gifted me, or one she'd bought specifically for me, or one of her own she wanted me to wear. She would tie a tight knot in the first layer, to ensure it wouldn't get untucked from the petticoat underneath. She would use the width of her hand as a guide to make all the pleats the same size. It was an art, and she had it down to a science.

I needed help getting dressed this time, because I just didn't want to deal with wrangling six yards of fabric with a frozen shoulder. So I asked Mom's best friend for help — I stood there with my arms out while Auntie pleated and tucked and pinned… and I thought about Mom the entire time.
Auntie didn't recognize the sari. Why would she? Mom had hundreds.
I told her it was Mom's.

For years, when RJ and I visited, we got the smaller bedroom upstairs. The bigger guest bedroom, with the bathroom attached, was my sister-in-law's — hers and her husband's and my niece's. It was just how everything worked.
That summer, we slept downstairs, in the primary bedroom. The biggest bedroom, the main bedroom. My in-laws’ bedroom.

Their mattress was old and too firm, and if we were going to live there for months, we owed ourselves at least some comfort. So we bought one of those Casper mattresses compressed in a box, from Costco, and it unrolled itself on their bed frame over the course of an afternoon.
That was the line, apparently. I would sleep in his parents' house, in his parents' room, under his parents' ceiling, doing his parents' paperwork. I just wouldn't sleep on their mattress.
It was the first thing in that house that was actually ours.

We unpacked everything. Not just out of the suitcases into piles, like we do on vacation, but into dresser drawers, into closets. We very quickly stopped pretending we were visiting. We were in it for the long haul.

Despite knowing we’d be living in that house for a while, we never made it ours. I made a calendar with photos of Kona and hung it in the living room, and that was more or less the extent of our decorating.

The houses on their street were new-ish builds, cookie-cutter. Not identical, but similar enough that I never figured out which neighbors lived in which house. If I hadn't known the house number, I'm not sure I could have picked Mom and Dad's out of a lineup. I needed the 18 on the mailbox and the flower planter by the door.
Even the house I was living in, I could only find by its labels.
I missed my stuff.
I missed my room. My shower. My soap.

I missed my lights. Nearly every bulb in Mom and Dad’s house was the cool, bluish kind. Every bulb in ours was warm. I didn't know that was something I cared about that much until I spent months eating dinner under cool lighting.

And I missed my kitchen, maybe most of all. It was small, with an island you could eat at — the type that every modern townhome has. It wasn’t special, it was builder grade, but it was mine. I knew where everything was, because I was the one who put it there. I had figured out my flow. My pots and pans, including my big red Le Creuset Dutch oven. My Bosch dishwasher that operated so quietly and got all my dishes sparkling clean. My spice cabinet. My pantry with my essentials. My mugs, my dinnerware, my utensils.

I am, it turns out, spoiled in Denver. I have the option of buying fresh, local everything, more or less whenever I want it. And anything that isn’t local is still pretty fresh due to living in a major city along major highways, and with a major airport (a lot of fish from Japan comes through Denver).

In suburban New Jersey, the nearest grocery store was a Stop & Shop, and the produce was, honestly, bad and sad. So the things I cooked were kind of bad and sad. OK, maybe not bad, but not nearly as good as I was used to. Pasta with ground meat and jarred tomato sauce. Meatballs. Salads. Stir fries, because I cannot go more than a few days without Asian food.
Mom's kitchen was perfectly fine. It just wasn't mine.
I remember eating a lot of pizza.
I missed my routine, too.
In Denver, mornings were a walk around the neighborhood with Kona, then coffee or tea, depending on the day, and a light breakfast at our dining table.

The Kona walk was the only part of the morning routine that made the trip east. She didn't care whose house it was, as long as somebody took her out. Any spot that was soft and cozy became her spot. Kona is, lucky for us, very adaptable. I am less so. The coffee was different, the tea was different, the breakfast was different. And there was no cute local coffee shop to walk to on the mornings I wanted a treat, because there was nothing to walk to at all.

On weekends in Denver, we saw friends. We went out to eat. We went to bakeries and breweries. We went to the farmers market most summer weekends. We went shopping at local boutiques. All of it in town, most of it close to our home. In suburban Jersey, everything required a car, and every errand turned into a commute. The grocery store, Target, the pet store — at least 15 minutes, often a half hour or more. The only things within 10 minutes were a bagel place and a pizza place in the nearest strip mall… which explains the pizza. At least the pizza was good.
We couldn't even walk Kona anywhere interesting. Just the cul-de-sacs, around and back.

My Denver friends would text, or we'd catch up on the phone, and so many of those conversations ended the same way: "Whenever you're back, let's hang out." Whenever. Nobody, including us, could say when that was.
We tried keeping a somewhat regular date night. But suburban date night is, as bougie as this sounds, kind of sad.

Some days, I didn't talk to anyone but RJ. Maybe a few little chats on Instagram, if I had the energy. Most nights ended on the couch with whatever was on — The Morning Show on Apple TV, the first season of Jury Duty — and then bed, and then the same day again.
A few things broke the loop.
In August, we drove to a dog-friendly beach park, just for a change of scenery and somewhere we could bring Kona.

A friend from college lived in the same township as my in-laws. We reconnected and went out for lunch at a Mediterranean place nearby. After months of doing things that were not easy, this was so easy — a breath of fresh air. I saw her once, maybe twice, the whole time I was there. We've been pretty close ever since.

And at some point, I decided to take up running. I have never liked running, not for a single stride of my life. But I needed to move my body, and moving needed to not be a task around the house. I ran around the cul-de-sacs, then around more of them — the same streets I walked Kona around, somehow at a much worse pace and with considerably more panting. I worked up to about three quarters of a mile, very slowly, and I have never done it again.
Summer turned into fall. The leaves turned. A few pumpkins showed up on doorsteps. It got cooler. Otherwise, the neighborhood looked exactly the same.
So did every day. Every one felt like a repeat. My suburban hell.
As if our lives weren’t stressful enough, we decided to sell our own house in Denver.
